title: Algorithms
description: Core algorithms from sorting to flows: when they apply and how they run.

entries.title: Binary Search
entries.summary: Halve a sorted range repeatedly to find a value or boundary in logarithmic time. Most uses are lower_bound-style boundary searches, not exact lookups.
entries.how_it_works: Maintain [lo, hi) with the invariant that the answer lies inside. Compare mid to the target and discard the half that cannot contain it. The range shrinks geometrically to one candidate.
pitfalls: (lo+hi)//2 overflow in fixed-width languages
Infinite loop from wrong branch updates
Searching unsorted data
tips: Use the [lo, hi) half-open shape uniformly
bisect module exists — know it, then reimplement for boundaries
Feasibility version powers pat.binary-search-answer

entries.title: Merge Sort
entries.summary: Split the array in half, sort each half, then merge two sorted runs in linear time. Stable, predictable O(n log n), and the template for divide-and-conquer counting.
entries.how_it_works: Recursively sort halves, then walk both with two fingers emitting the smaller head each step. The merge is linear because each comparison permanently places one element.
pitfalls: <= vs < changes stability
Slicing copies cost memory; fine for learning
Recursion depth on huge inputs in some languages
tips: Add a counter in merge to count inversions
Bottom-up version avoids recursion
Timsort (Python's sorted) is merge+insertion hybrid

entries.title: Quicksort and Quickselect
entries.summary: Partition around a pivot so smaller elements go left, then recurse. The same partition step gives quickselect for k-th order statistics in average linear time.
entries.how_it_works: Choose a pivot, rearrange so left < pivot <= right, recurse on both sides. Quickselect recurses into only the side containing k. Random pivots make worst cases vanishingly unlikely.

complexity.time: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst; quickselect O(n) average

entries.example:
import random
def quickselect(a, k):
    # k-th smallest, 0-based; mutates a
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while True:
        p = a[random.randint(lo, hi)]
        i, j = lo, hi
        while i <= j:
            while a[i] < p: i += 1
            while a[j] > p: j -= 1
            if i <= j:
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]; i += 1; j -= 1
        if j < k: lo = i
        elif k < i: hi = j
        else: return a[k]
pitfalls: Fixed pivot (first/last) degrades on sorted input
3-way partition needed for many duplicates
Worst-case recursion depth
tips: Random pivot or shuffle first
Quickselect > full sort for top-k
Dutch-national-flag partition handles duplicates

entries.title: Breadth-First Search
entries.summary: Explore a graph layer by layer with a queue, giving shortest paths in unweighted graphs. The visited set is the whole algorithm — without it, BFS loops forever.
recognize: Shortest path with uniform edge cost
entries.how_it_works: Push the start with distance 0, mark visited. Pop front, relax unvisited neighbors with distance+1 and push them. First visit to a node is via a shortest path because the queue is FIFO.
pitfalls: Marking visited at pop time instead of push time (queue blowup)
Using BFS on weighted edges
Forgetting disconnected components need outer loop
tips: 0-1 BFS (deque) handles weights {0,1}
Bidirectional BFS halves exponential blowup
Grid BFS: encode (r, c) or flatten index

entries.title: Depth-First Search
entries.summary: Plunge down each path with a stack (or recursion) before backtracking. Entry/exit timestamps classify edges and power topo-sort, cycle detection, and connected components.
entries.how_it_works: Visit a node, recursively visit each unvisited neighbor, then finish. The recursion stack is the current path: a neighbor already on the stack means a directed cycle. Finish times in decreasing order give topo-sort.
pitfalls: Recursion limit on deep graphs (sys.setrecursionlimit or iterative)
Gray/black coloring needed for directed cycles
Stack overflow on path graphs
tips: Colors: 0 unvisited, 1 in-stack, 2 done
Iterative DFS with explicit stack for huge graphs
Finish-time order is free topo-sort (see pat.toposort-pattern)

entries.title: Topological Sort
entries.summary: Linearly order a DAG so every edge points forward; impossible exactly when a cycle exists. The workhorse behind scheduling and DAG DP.
entries.how_it_works: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes indegree-0 nodes. DFS variant emits nodes in decreasing finish time. Either way, leftover nodes prove a cycle.
entries.example:
# See pat.toposort-pattern for the full Kahn implementation.
# DFS one-liner idea:
#   order.append(u) AFTER exploring neighbors, then reverse(order)
pitfalls: Applying to cyclic graphs silently
Assuming uniqueness
Confusing topo order with sorted node labels
tips: Any DAG DP goes: topo order, then relax once
Use a heap for lexicographically smallest order
See the pattern entry for the complete template

entries.title: KMP String Matching
entries.summary: Precompute the prefix function so a mismatch slides the pattern forward instead of restarting. String search becomes linear in text plus pattern.
entries.how_it_works: pi[i] = longest proper prefix of pattern[..i] that is also a suffix. On mismatch at pattern position j, jump to pi[j-1] instead of 0 — the overlap already matched is reused, never rescanned.
pitfalls: Forgetting the while fallback loop (single if is wrong)
Overlapping matches need continued fallback, not reset
pi values are lengths, index with j-1
tips: pi[last] gives the minimal period: n - pi[n-1]
Z-algorithm is the alternative with the same complexity
Automata view: pi edges are fallback transitions

entries.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
entries.summary: Grow shortest paths outward always settling the unsettled node with smallest tentative distance. Correct for non-negative weights; a min-heap makes it fast.
entries.how_it_works: Pop the minimum-distance unsettled node; its distance is final because any alternative route must pass through an unsettled node at least as far. Relax its edges and push updates. Stale heap entries are skipped on pop.

complexity.time: O((V + E) log V) with binary heap

pitfalls: Negative weights (use Bellman-Ford)
Missing the stale-entry skip (still correct, much slower)
Not stopping early when only one target is needed
tips: Early exit when the target pops
State graphs (node, extra) model constraints like keys
Dial's bucket variant for small integer weights

entries.title: Bellman-Ford
entries.summary: Relax every edge V-1 times to handle negative weights, then one more pass to expose negative cycles. Slower than Dijkstra but strictly more general.
entries.how_it_works: After k rounds, distances reflect paths of at most k edges; V-1 rounds suffice for simple paths. If round V still improves anything, a reachable negative cycle exists.
pitfalls: Only detects cycles reachable from the source (add super-source for all)
INF + w overflow in fixed-width languages
Early-break flag must reset each round
tips: SPFA is a faster average-case variant with worst-case traps
Super-source with 0 edges reaches every component
Difference constraints x_v <= x_u + w are Bellman-Ford directly

entries.title: Floyd-Warshall
entries.summary: All-pairs shortest paths by DP over intermediate vertices: try routing through k for every pair. Three lines, cubic time, handles negatives (no negative cycles).
recognize: All-pairs distances, dense or small graphs
entries.how_it_works: dist[i][j] starts as the direct edge. For each k, allow paths through k: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]). After all k, every pair uses the best intermediates.
pitfalls: k must be the OUTER loop
INF + INF overflow in fixed-width languages
Mutating the caller's matrix
tips: Negative diagonal after run means negative cycle
Same skeleton gives transitive closure (or/and) and minimax paths
Johnson's beats it on sparse graphs

entries.title: Kruskal's MST
entries.summary: Sort all edges by weight and greedily add each edge that connects two different components. The cut property guarantees each addition is safe.
entries.how_it_works: Union-find tracks components. Processing edges light-first, an edge joining two components must cross some cut as its lightest edge, so it belongs to an MST. Skip edges inside one component.
pitfalls: Disconnected graph (taken < n-1 check)
Forgetting path compression/halving
Equal weights: any MST is fine, don't over-constrain
tips: Maximum spanning tree: sort descending
MST bottleneck property powers minimax-path queries
Boruvka/Prim win on dense graphs

entries.title: LCA with Binary Lifting
entries.summary: Precompute 2^k-th ancestors so any node jumps up in powers of two; lift the deeper node, then both together. Distance and k-th ancestor queries come free.
entries.how_it_works: up[k][v] = 2^k-th ancestor, built by doubling. Equalize depths, then from large k down, lift both while ancestors differ; their parents meet at the LCA. dist(u,v) = depth[u]+depth[v]-2*depth[lca].

complexity.time: O((N + Q) log N) preprocess, O(log N) per query

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE:
  dfs from root: depth[v], up[0][v] = parent
  up[k][v] = up[k-1][ up[k-1][v] ]
  lca(u, v):
    if depth[u] < depth[v]: swap
    lift u up to depth[v]
    if u == v: return u
    for k descending: if up[k][u] != up[k][v]: u, v = up[k][u], up[k][v]
    return parent[u]
pitfalls: Root's ancestors must point to root/0 consistently
Forgetting to equalize depths first
LOG too small for N (need ceil(log2(N))+1)
tips: Euler tour + RMQ is the O(1)-query alternative
Same table answers k-th ancestor
Works on forests with a super-root

entries.title: Convex Hull Trick
entries.summary: Query the minimum of many lines at x fast by keeping only the lower envelope. Sorted slopes give O(1) amortized queries; Li Chao trees handle arbitrary order in O(log C).
recognize: DP of form dp[i] = min_j (m_j * x_i + b_j)
entries.how_it_works: Each line is best on one x-interval; worse lines are discarded. With increasing slopes and queries, a deque maintains the envelope and queries pop from the front. Li Chao inserts a line into segment-tree nodes covering where it wins.

complexity.time: O(1) amortized monotone, O(log C) Li Chao

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE monotone CHT (min, increasing slopes, increasing x):
  deque holds (m, b); bad(l1, l2, l3) if l2 never minimal
  add_line(m, b): while len>=2 and bad(deq[-2], deq[-1], (m,b)): pop; append
  query(x): while len>=2 and value(front, x) >= value(next, x): popleft; return value(front, x)
pitfalls: Sign errors flipping min/max or slope order
Equal slopes: keep only the better intercept
Overflow in intersection tests (use cross-multiplication)
tips: Li Chao tree when nothing is sorted
Divide-and-conquer offline variant also exists
Verify monotonicity; else fall back to Li Chao

entries.title: Max Flow / Min Cut
entries.summary: The maximum flow equals the minimum cut capacity. Bipartite matching, closure, and segmentation problems are flows in disguise — model first, algorithm second.
recognize: Min cut to separate source from sink
entries.how_it_works: Repeatedly push flow along residual paths; when none remain, reachable vertices from the source define a cut whose capacity equals the flow, proving optimality. Always add reverse edges to allow undo.

complexity.time: Depends on method; Dinic is the default choice

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE Ford-Fulkerson skeleton:
  build residual graph with reverse edge capacity 0 for each edge
  loop:
    find s-t path in residual graph (BFS/DFS)
    if none: break  (flow is optimal by min-cut)
    push bottleneck capacity; update forward/reverse edges
  reachable set from s = source side of min cut
pitfalls: Forgetting reverse edges
Using DFS augmenting paths on big capacities (too slow)
Modeling errors: capacities on wrong edges
tips: Bipartite matching = source/sink + unit edges
Min cutfrom max flow gives the actual partition
Dinic (alg.dinic) is the implementation to learn

entries.title: Dinic's Algorithm
entries.summary: BFS builds level layers, then DFS pushes blocking flows that saturate at least one edge per path. Phases make it dramatically faster than naive augmenting paths.
entries.how_it_works: Level graph via BFS from source; DFS sends flow only forward in levels, with current-arc pointers skipping dead edges. Each blocking flow finishes a phase; O(V) phases suffice, fewer on unit networks.

complexity.time: O(V^2 E) general; O(E sqrt(V)) on unit networks

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE:
  loop:
    BFS levels from s; if t unreachable: break
    reset current-arc pointers
    while (pushed = dfs(s, t, INF)) > 0: flow += pushed
  dfs(u, t, f):
    if u == t: return f
    for each edge u->v with cap>0 and level[v]==level[u]+1 (from current arc):
      pushed = dfs(v, t, min(f, cap)); update residual; if pushed: return pushed
    return 0
pitfalls: Recursion depth on long paths (raise limit or go iterative)
Not resetting current arcs each phase
int vs float capacities
tips: Scaling + capacity tricks rarely needed after Dinic
Bipartite matching via Dinic beats Hopcroft-Karp to write
Push-relabel is the alternative for huge graphs

entries.title: Suffix Array and LCP
entries.summary: Sort all suffixes to enable binary-searched substring queries; Kasai's LCP array adds longest-common-prefix power. Doubling construction is the practical O(n log n) route.
entries.how_it_works: Rank single chars, then repeatedly sort by (rank[i], rank[i+k]) pairs doubling k, compressing ranks each round. Kasai walks suffixes in text order maintaining that LCP drops by at most 1 between steps.

complexity.time: O(n log n) doubling; Kasai O(n)

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE doubling:
  rank = [ord(c) for c in s]; k = 1; sa = range(n)
  while True:
    sort sa by (rank[i], rank[i+k] if i+k < n else -1)
    new_rank[sa[0]] = 0
    for t in 1..n-1: new_rank[sa[t]] = new_rank[sa[t-1]] + (pair differs ? 1 : 0)
    rank = new_rank; if max rank == n-1: break; k *= 2
pitfalls: Sentinel handling for i+k >= n (-1 rank)
Not recompressing ranks each round
Kasai needs inverse (rank[pos]) array first
tips: Suffix automaton/trie is better for online substring queries
LCP + RMQ answers longest-common-substring queries
Library doubling is fine; SA-IS is overkill

entries.title: FFT and NTT
entries.summary: Multiply polynomials (and big integers, and convolutions) in O(n log n) by evaluating at roots of unity, pointwise-multiplying, and interpolating back. NTT is the exact modular version.
recognize: Mod prime NTT (998244353) to stay exact
entries.how_it_works: FFT evaluates a degree-n polynomial at n roots of unity in O(n log n) via even/odd split. Convolution becomes pointwise products in value form; inverse FFT returns coefficients. NTT repeats the same dance in a finite field with a primitive root.
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE iterative FFT:
  bit-reverse permute a
  length = 2, 4, 8, ... :
    w = root of unity for this length (and inverse on way back)
    for each block: butterfly combine pairs (u, v) -> (u+v, u+v*w)
  divide by n after inverse transform
  convolution(a, b) = inverse(fft(a) * fft(b)) pointwise
pitfalls: Float rounding on huge coefficients (use NTT or splitting)
Forgetting bit-reversal or the final /n
Wrong primitive root for NTT modulus
tips: 998244353 is NTT-friendly; 1e9+7 is not
Naive O(n^2) wins below ~64 elements
Three-mod CRT recovers results for arbitrary moduli

entries.title: Heavy-Light Decomposition
entries.summary: Split a tree into heavy paths so any root path crosses O(log n) segments, each a contiguous array range. Path queries become segment-tree queries.
entries.how_it_works: First DFS sizes subtrees; each node's heavy child is the largest. Decompose so heavy edges stay in one chain with contiguous positions. Climb chain by chain: query the segment within each chain, jump to its head's parent.
pitfalls: Edge values live on child positions, not the LCA's
Forgetting to swap so u is deeper
Euler-tour subtree ranges need separate handling
tips: Binary lifting (alg.lca) is simpler when only LCAs are needed
Fenwick suffices for point-update path-sum
Test on stars, paths, and caterpillars

entries.title: Centroid Decomposition
entries.summary: Repeatedly remove the centroid (whose removal leaves components of size <= n/2) to build a log-depth centroid tree. Path-through-centroid queries decompose any tree path.
recognize: Counting paths with a constraint (length, xor, sum)
Dynamic tree queries via centroid ancestors
entries.how_it_works: Find the centroid, solve all paths passing through it with local structures, mark removed, recurse on components. Every node has O(log n) centroid ancestors, so queries walk up that chain.

complexity.time: O(n log n) build; O(log n) per query step
complexity.space: O(n log n) worst case, often O(n)

entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE decompose(entry, size):
  c = find centroid of entry's component
  mark c removed; parent_centroid[c] = current
  process all paths through c with a frequency structure
  for each unremoved neighbor: decompose(neighbor, component size)
query(v): walk centroid ancestors of v combining local answers
pitfalls: Recomputing sizes without respecting removed flags
Double-counting paths (subtract same-subtree contributions)
Recursion depth on skewed centroid chains
tips: Classic first problem: count pairs with distance <= K
DSU-on-tree is the alternative for subtree queries
HLD (alg.hld) covers path aggregates instead

entries.title: Knuth Optimization
entries.summary: For interval DP with quadrangle inequality and monotonicity, the optimal split for [i, j] lies between the optima of [i, j-1] and [i+1, j]. Searching only that range drops O(n^3) to O(n^2).
recognize: DP over intervals with split cost C[i][j]
Optimal binary search tree / optimal merge pattern
D&C optimization applies but bounds are tighter
entries.how_it_works: Keep opt[i][j], the argmin split. Monotonicity (opt[i][j-1] <= opt[i][j] <= opt[i+1][j]) narrows each search to a slice; total work per diagonal is O(n). Requires quadrangle inequality plus monotonicity of C.
entries.example:
PSEUDOCODE (length increasing):
  dp[i][i] = base; opt[i][i] = i
  for length in 2..n:
    for i in 1..n-length+1:
      j = i + length - 1
      dp[i][j] = min over k in [opt[i][j-1], opt[i+1][j]] of (dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j]) + C[i][j]
      opt[i][j] = argmin k
pitfalls: Applying without quadrangle inequality (silently wrong)
Off-by-one in the opt range bounds
C must also be monotone in the right sense
tips: Optimal BST and stone merging are the textbook cases
Strictly stronger than D&C optimization when it applies
Verify the inequalities on paper first
